title: Revenue By Discount Tier
category: CASE & Conditional Logic (Bucketing a Float Column)
outcome: 🆕 new practice question — not attempted yet
watchOutFor: discount is a REAL: 0.05 is stored as 0.0500000007, so `discount <= 0.05` is false. Use half-open ranges.
problem: Finance wants to know whether larger discounts actually drive bigger orders, by comparing order lines in each discount tier.
objective: Bucket order lines into No discount, Under 10%, 10% to under 15%, and 15% or more; show lines, units, net revenue (2 dp) and average quantity (1 dp) per tier, in tier order.
expectedOutput:
| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| discount_tier | Tier label, numbered so it sorts correctly |
| order_lines | Number of order lines |
| units | Total quantity |
| net_revenue | SUM(unit_price × quantity × (1 − discount)), 2 dp |
| avg_quantity | Average quantity per line, 1 dp |

| discount_tier | order_lines | units | net_revenue | avg_quantity |
|---------------|-------------|-------|-------------|--------------|
| 1. No discount | 100 | 1920 | 48442.75 | 19.2 |
| 2. Under 10% | 50 | 1000 | 33669.89 | 20.0 |
| 3. 10% to under 15% | 50 | 1080 | 33360.69 | 21.6 |
| 4. 15% or more | 50 | 1080 | 22846.47 | 21.6 |

*(Sample rows are illustrative — the first few rows from the practice dataset, shown to convey shape/format; your data instance may differ.)*
approach:
1. CASE with half-open ranges: = 0, < 0.1, < 0.15, else.
2. GROUP BY 1 groups by the CASE expression.
3. Number the labels so ORDER BY discount_tier sorts them in tier order.
mySolution:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN discount = 0    THEN '1. No discount'
         WHEN discount < 0.1  THEN '2. Under 10%'
         WHEN discount < 0.15 THEN '3. 10% to under 15%'
         ELSE                      '4. 15% or more'
       END                                                          AS discount_tier,
       COUNT(*)                                                     AS order_lines,
       SUM(quantity)                                                AS units,
       ROUND(SUM(unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount))::numeric, 2) AS net_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(quantity), 1)                                      AS avg_quantity
FROM order_details
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY discount_tier;

referenceQuery:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN discount = 0    THEN '1. No discount'
         WHEN discount < 0.1  THEN '2. Under 10%'
         WHEN discount < 0.15 THEN '3. 10% to under 15%'
         ELSE                      '4. 15% or more'
       END                                                          AS discount_tier,
       COUNT(*)                                                     AS order_lines,
       SUM(quantity)                                                AS units,
       ROUND(SUM(unit_price * quantity * (1 - discount))::numeric, 2) AS net_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(quantity), 1)                                      AS avg_quantity
FROM order_details
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY discount_tier;
why: CASE checks its branches top to bottom and stops at the first match, so each branch only needs an upper bound. The discount column is REAL (floating point): 0.05 is stored slightly above 0.05, so a boundary like `<= 0.05` silently moves lines into the next tier. Half-open ranges (`< 0.1`) put every stored value in exactly one tier.
pitfalls: Using <= on float boundaries, which misplaces values stored just above the boundary.
Forgetting ELSE, which turns unexpected values into NULL tiers.
Ordering by the label text without a prefix, which sorts '15% or more' before 'No discount'.

followups.question: How would you avoid float issues entirely?
followups.answer: Store discounts as NUMERIC(4,3), or compare ROUND(discount::numeric, 3).

followups.question: How would you show tiers with no lines?
followups.answer: Generate the tier list in a VALUES list and LEFT JOIN the grouped result to it.

followups.question: How would you show each tier's share of revenue?
followups.answer: Add ROUND(100 * SUM(...) / SUM(SUM(...)) OVER (), 1) as a window over the grouped rows.

takeaway: Bucket with half-open ranges, especially on floating-point columns; boundaries with = are fragile.
